procedural_history.impugned_order: Final judgment and order dated 23rd July 2019, passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Confirmation Case No. 2 of 2016 filed by the State of Maharashtra, by which it upheld the separate orders of conviction and sentence dated 26th August 2016 and 31st August 2016 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge, Pune1 in Sessions
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Bombay upheld the order of the trial court convicting the appellant and also confirmed the death sentence imposed on him in Confirmation Case No. 2 of 2016. The operation of the High Court's judgment was stayed pending appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's judgment, filed a criminal appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 213 of 2020) in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed and set aside the judgment and order of the High Court dated 23rd July 2019 in Confirmation Case No. 2 of 2016 and the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 26th August 2016 and 31st August 2016 passed by the trial court in Sessions Case No.64 of 2013.

directions: The judgment and order of the High Court dated 23rd July 2019 in Confirmation Case No. 2 of 2016 and the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 26th August 2016 and 31st August 2016 passed by the trial court in Sessions Case No.64 of 2013 are quashed and set aside;
The appellant is directed to be set at liberty if not required in any other case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant for offences under Sections 302, 307, and 201 of the IPC was sustainable based on the evidence on record.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's judgment was flawed as it relied on a circumstance that the court itself had disbelieved in its judgment.
Medical evidence was not properly appreciated, specifically a case paper (Exhibit 93-A) which indicated that the appellant was conscious and oriented.
The opinion of the doctor who first examined the patient, an important person for determining the nature of injuries, was not given sufficient weight.

cases.case_name: Chuhar Singh v. State of Haryana
cases.principle: For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency.

cases.case_name: Sharad Birdhichand Sharda v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must fully establish a chain of evidence so complete that it is conclusive in nature, consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt, and excludes every other possible hypothesis. The circumstances must not be explainable on any other hypothesis except the guilt of the accused, and must show that in all human probability, the act was done by the accused. The standard of proof is that the accused 'must be' proven guilty, not merely 'may be' proven guilty.
obiter: There is not only a grammatical but a legal distinction between ‘may be proved’ and ‘must be or should be proved’.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the prosecution's case, which was left with only the circumstance of motive, was insufficient for a conviction. A conviction cannot be based solely on motive, as suspicion, no matter how strong, cannot substitute for proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The prosecution failed to meet the high standard of proof required in a circumstantial evidence case, specifically the principle that the accused 'must be' and not merely 'may be' guilty, and that every possible hypothesis except the guilt of theaccused has to be ruled out.
legal_tests_applied: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn must be fully established.
The facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and should not be explainable on any other hypothesis.
The circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency, excluding every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.

There must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.
There is a legal distinction between what 'may be proved' and what 'must be or should be proved'; the accused 'must be' and not merely 'may be' guilty before a court can convict.
A suspicion, however strong it may be, cannot take the place of a proof beyond reasonable doubt.
policy_considerations: It is a primary principle of criminal justice that an accused person 'must be' and not merely 'may be' guilty before a court can convict them, ensuring a high standard of proof to prevent wrongful convictions based on suspicion.
